On May 22, 1796 it staged André Grétry's Sylvain, the first opera known to have been performed in the city, which began an operatic tradition that New Orleans kept up almost without a break. The composer Joseph Arquier worked in the city from 1800 to 1803. The building is long gone and the point marks the block where it stood, not a surviving structure. Sources differ on the end: 64 Parishes says the theatre closed in 1803, while another account has it shut that year for repairs, reopened in 1804 and finally auctioned off in 1810.

new_value: Union Sons Hall, at 1319 Perdido Street, was one of the busiest dance halls in the Black back-of-town district that the whites-only Storyville excluded. Around 1900 its biggest draw was cornetist Buddy Bolden, whose loud, bluesy, improvised playing is the earliest documented New Orleans jazz. His band played late into the night and cleared out in time for the First Lincoln Baptist Church to hold Sunday services in the same room. The nickname comes from the Bolden tune also known as Buddy Bolden's Blues. Louis Armstrong, who grew up nearby, remembered hearing Bolden here. The building was torn down in the mid-1950s, when the block was cleared for the present City Hall.
